design_detail: Two-part review. (1) A narrative review of meta-analyses and selected studies on alcohol and ischaemic heart disease (IHD): the reference group, average intake, drinking pattern, confounding by age, smoking and other factors, short-term experimental and Mendelian randomization evidence. (2) A systematic review and DerSimonian–Laird random-effects meta-analysis of seven observational studies comparing drinkers averaging under 30 g/day, with and without episodic heavy drinking, against lifetime abstainers. Searches from 1980 to August 2014 following PRISMA; the databases, search strings, protocols and details of the seven studies are only in Additional file 1 (not read). As the round brief directs, AMSTAR 2 is applied to the systematic part; the narrative part is described in the reasoning against the editors' narrative-review checklist.
can_establish: From part 2: the pooled IHD association, against lifetime abstainers, of drinking under 30 g/day on average without heavy drinking occasions and of the same average intake with such occasions, in seven published observational studies. From part 1: the authors' reading of the meta-analytic literature to 2014, much of it their own.
cannot_establish: That drinking without heavy episodes lowers IHD risk (observational studies without a risk-of-bias appraisal; the experimental evidence cited is short-term and on surrogate markers); which studies, designs, participants and heavy-drinking thresholds lie behind the pooled estimates (given only in the supplement); and, from part 1, any systematic or appraised synthesis (meta-analyses are selected and summarized without a stated method).

sample.recruitment: Two searches of electronic databases from 1980 to the second week of August (2014 according to the abstract): one for meta-analyses on alcohol and IHD, one for original articles (letters, editorials, conference abstracts, reviews and comments excluded), plus hand-searching of the references of identified papers and of relevant reviews and meta-analyses. The databases and search terms are given only in Additional file 1 (Methods › Searches).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Meta-analysis: adult (18 or over) population samples; IHD as a separate outcome (ICD-9 410–414, ICD-10 I20–I25); case-control, prospective or historical cohort design; average intake over a reference period of more than 2 weeks; a drinking group averaging under 30 g/day that specifically excluded or included episodic heavy drinking; a risk measure against lifetime abstainers with its variability (or data to compute it); English, German or Spanish. Excluded: self-reported IHD and samples of people with IHD-related conditions (Methods › Meta-analysis › Inclusion and exclusion criteria).
sample.demographics: Not reported in the article (Table S1 of Additional file 1, not read). All seven studies adjusted for age and smoking, five for education or other socio-economic indicators, and four each for body mass index and marital status (Results and discussion › Meta-analysis on drinking pattern among moderate alcohol drinkers, 1st paragraph).
sample.selection_effects: Single-author search and data extraction; languages limited to English, German and Spanish without a stated reason; grey literature excluded; primary authors not contacted when data were missing. Only seven studies met the criteria, and their identities, designs, settings and sizes are not given in the article. The legend of Figure 2 marks one of its entries as taken from the authors' 2010 meta-analysis; how far the seven studies overlap with that review is not stated.

exposure.measurement: Self-reported average intake over more than 2 weeks, with a measure of heavy drinking occasions, as defined by each primary study; the threshold for a heavy drinking occasion is not stated in the article (Methods › Meta-analysis › Inclusion and exclusion criteria).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Two exposure groups, each against lifetime abstainers: average under 30 g/day without heavy drinking occasions, and the same average with such occasions. In the narrative, chronic heavy drinking means an average of 60 g/day or more; the conclusions speak of one to two drinks per drinking day without heavy episodes, without defining a drink.
exposure.polysubstance: Smoking was adjusted for in all seven studies; smoking as an effect modifier is discussed narratively (the evidence in smokers is called mixed). Other drug use is not addressed.

comparison.controls: Lifetime abstainers (former drinkers not included). Where needed, within-study estimates were re-expressed against lifetime abstainers by the method of Hamling et al., with priority given to estimates already comparing drinkers with lifetime abstainers (Methods › Meta-analysis › Data abstraction and Statistical analysis).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Differences between lifetime abstainers and drinkers beyond the covariates listed (health, social position, reasons for not drinking); the narrative itself cites a US study showing that non-drinkers differ in their reasons for not drinking in ways that the lifetime-abstainer and former-drinker split may not capture (Results and discussion › Lifetime abstainers and former drinkers).

outcomes.instruments: IHD (ICD-9 410–414; ICD-10 I20–I25), mortality and morbidity combined, called IHD incidence (Figure 2 legend; Results and discussion › Average alcohol consumption, 3rd paragraph).
outcomes.validity_norms: No risk-of-bias assessment of the seven studies is described; the article calls them high-quality and well adjusted.
outcomes.operationalization: Hazard ratios, odds ratios and relative risks treated as equivalent; the most-adjusted estimate was used, giving priority to comparisons with lifetime abstainers, and information from related papers on the same cohort was used where possible (Methods › Meta-analysis › Data abstraction and Statistical analysis).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Two pooled estimates (without and with heavy drinking occasions) and their ratio.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. The first author performed the literature search and abstracted the data; full-text articles of potential eligibility were discussed by both authors until consensus (Methods › Meta-analysis › Data abstraction).

analysis.effect_sizes: DerSimonian–Laird random-effects pooling on the natural log scale, Cochran's Q and I², Egger's test, and leave-one-out sensitivity analysis (Methods › Meta-analysis › Statistical analysis). Against lifetime abstainers: drinkers averaging under 30 g/day without heavy drinking occasions, RR 0.64 (95% CI 0.53 to 0.71), I² 10%; with heavy drinking occasions, 1.12 (0.91 to 1.37), I² 0%; Egger P = 0.35 and 0.58; no single study had a large influence. Ratio between the two groups 1.75 (1.36 to 2.25). The numbers of participants and events are not given in the article.
analysis.covariates: None at review level; most-adjusted estimates, all adjusted at least for age and smoking.
analysis.preregistration_detail: The article does not mention registration; Additional file 1 is described as containing the systematic review protocols for the narrative and quantitative reviews (not read), and the authors' contributions mention protocol design.
analysis.selective_reporting: The meta-analysis is reported in two paragraphs, with the study details in the supplement. In the narrative, the authors' own 2012 meta-analysis is represented by its all-studies estimates only (see interpretation gap).
analysis.power: Not addressed. With seven studies, Egger's test has little power to detect small-study effects (editors' note), which the article does not discuss.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Part 2: in seven observational studies, drinkers averaging under 30 g/day without heavy drinking occasions had a lower pooled IHD risk than lifetime abstainers (0.64), while those with the same average intake and heavy drinking occasions did not differ from lifetime abstainers (1.12, 0.91 to 1.37). Part 1 reports, mostly from the authors' own meta-analyses: higher IHD mortality in former drinkers than in lifetime abstainers (women 1.54, men 1.25); no lower IHD risk in men drinking 60 g/day or more against lifetime abstainers (mortality 1.00, 0.74 to 1.36); and higher IHD mortality in people treated for alcohol use disorder than in the general population (men 1.62, women 2.09).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that the epidemiological evidence for a beneficial effect of low intake without heavy drinking episodes is strong and corroborated by experiments, and the conclusions say the alcohol–IHD relationship fulfils all of Hill's criteria for causation (Conclusions, 2nd paragraph). Gaps: (1) the quantitative support is a seven-study meta-analysis with single-author selection and extraction and no risk-of-bias assessment, whose studies are not named in the article; (2) the experimental evidence is short-term studies of surrogate markers such as HDL cholesterol, which, as the authors note, is highest in people with alcohol use disorder; (3) the narrative reports the authors' 2012 meta-analysis through its all-studies estimates (0.69 to 0.81, all significant, at 1–2 drinks a day) and does not mention that its sex- and end point-stratified estimates for men's IHD mortality at about 1 and 2 drinks were not significant, or that its abstract said cardioprotection could not be assumed for all drinkers; (4) the Mendelian randomization study of Holmes et al. (2014), which found no protective effect, is set aside because the genetic variant was also associated with less binge drinking, and readers are referred to the authors' own rapid response to that paper; (5) the evidence on confounding is a selection of stratified studies, not a systematic synthesis. The conclusions also say that no amount of drinking is safe and that starting to drink should not be considered as prevention, which stands beside the causal claim without resolving it.

timeline.event: Roerecke & Rehm (American Journal of Epidemiology): among current drinkers who were not chronic heavy drinkers, heavy drinking occasions were associated with higher IHD risk than regular moderate drinking (RR 1.45, 1.24 to 1.70); the legend of Figure 2 of this review marks an entry as taken from it.
Ruidavets et al. (BMJ), the PRIME study of drinking patterns and IHD in France and Northern Ireland, cited here as showing similar findings.
Roerecke & Rehm (American Journal of Epidemiology): former drinkers had higher IHD mortality than lifetime abstainers (women 1.54, men 1.25).
Roerecke & Rehm (Addiction): average intake and IHD against lifetime abstainers by sex and end point (read in this round; card sc_roerecke_2012).
Roerecke & Rehm (Open Heart): chronic heavy drinking (60 g/day or more) showed no lower IHD risk than lifetime abstention (mortality 1.00, 0.74 to 1.36; incidence 1.04, 0.83 to 1.31).

Holmes et al. (BMJ) Mendelian randomization analysis concluding there was no protective effect; Rehm & Roerecke posted a rapid response to it on the BMJ site, cited here as ref. 97. Holmes et al. is read in this round by another reader.
This review: drinkers under 30 g/day without heavy episodes 0.64 against lifetime abstainers; with heavy episodes 1.12.

replication.where_it_stands: The pattern finding, that heavy drinking occasions remove the lower IHD risk seen in light drinkers, rests on this team's own meta-analyses (2010 and this one, which may share studies) and was not independently replicated in the sources read. The causal reading of the low-intake association is contested by genetic studies. The review can be cited for its pattern contrast, with its comparator (lifetime abstainers) and its limits, and as a pointer to the authors' other meta-analyses; its narrative conclusions are the authors' judgment, not findings.

funding.funder: European Community's Seventh Framework Programme (FP7/2007-2013), Grant Agreement no. 266813, Addictions and Lifestyle in Contemporary Europe – Reframing Addictions Project (ALICE RAP); the views are stated to be the authors' only (Acknowledgments).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare that they have no competing interests (Competing interests). In the same authors' 2012 meta-analysis, J. Rehm had declared taking part in scientific meetings organized or sponsored by the alcohol industry with financial support for that participation; no such statement appears here.
funding.affiliations_note: Centre for Addiction and Mental Health and the University of Toronto (Dalla Lana School of Public Health, Institute of Medical Science, Department of Psychiatry), and TU Dresden. The narrative rests mainly on the authors' own meta-analyses (refs 15, 26, 33, 39 and 42); Figure 1 is built from three of them (refs 15, 33 and 39) plus the Russian studies.

what_would_settle_it: Prospective cohorts with lifetime drinking histories and repeated measures of both average intake and heavy drinking occasions, separating lifetime abstainers, former and occasional drinkers, pooled at the individual level under a registered protocol; with genetic analyses designed to separate average volume from drinking pattern. Causation at low intake would need a long-term trial, which the authors consider unavailable.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (adult population samples), exposure (drinking under 30 g/day with or without heavy drinking occasions), comparator (lifetime abstainers), outcome (IHD by ICD codes) and designs are specified.
Provisional: the article does not say whether a protocol was registered or fixed in advance; Additional file 1, not read, is described as holding the review protocols.
Case-control and cohort designs; the background explains that long-term randomized trials are missing and will remain so.

The databases and search terms are only in the supplement, but the article itself shows an unjustified restriction to English, German and Spanish and the exclusion of letters, editorials, conference abstracts, reviews and comments; no grey literature or expert contact, and primary authors were not contacted for missing data. Under the project's reading of item 4 this is no whatever the supplement shows.
The first author performed the literature search; only full texts of potential eligibility were discussed by both authors.
The first author abstracted the data alone.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: No list of excluded studies in the article, and the supplement's described contents (protocols, two search-results figures, a table of the seven included studies, two forest plots) do not include one.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Provisional: the included studies are described only in Table S1 of the supplement (not read); the article gives only the covariates adjusted for.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: No method for assessing the risk of bias of the included studies is described; the studies are called high-quality and well adjusted without an appraisal.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported

domains.note: Random-effects pooling on the log scale of most-adjusted estimates against lifetime abstainers, with within-study re-referencing by the method of Hamling et al.; heterogeneity was low. The method behind the ratio of 1.75 between the two groups, whose estimates share reference groups, is not described.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No analysis of the impact of risk of bias on the pooled estimates; only leave-one-out analyses.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The abstract calls the evidence strong and the conclusions call the relationship causal by Hill's criteria, without considering the risk of bias of the seven pooled studies, which was never assessed; the narrative discussion of confounding concerns the literature in general. A close call, since confounding is discussed at length.
Egger's test for both pools (P = 0.35 and 0.58), reported as no evidence of publication bias; with seven studies the test has little power, which is not discussed.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding (EU Seventh Framework Programme, ALICE RAP) and a statement of no competing interests are reported.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Systematic part (the meta-analysis of drinking pattern): four critical items are not met (4, search; 7, excluded studies; 9, risk-of-bias assessment; 13, interpretation), so confidence is critically low. Items 2 and 8 are provisional (judged no information because they depend on a supplement not read), but they cannot change the overall rating, which is therefore not provisional. Single-author screening and extraction and a description of the studies only in the supplement add to the concern. Narrative part (not scored by AMSTAR 2; the editors' narrative-review checklist, for information): systematic search and explicit selection, some concerns (a search for meta-analyses is reported, but which ones are discussed, and why, is not explained); appraisal of the cited studies, high concerns (none); reliance on the authors' own studies, high (most quantitative statements and Figure 1 come from the authors' own meta-analyses); separation of evidence from speculation, some concerns (the Russian adjustments are labelled speculation, but causal conclusions are stated as findings); balance between evidence for and against a protective effect of low intake, some concerns, with the evidence against (the authors' own stratified 2012 estimates; the genetic study) under-represented. The review can be cited for its pattern contrast as reported, with its comparator, and for pointers; its causal statements are the authors' judgment.

key_findings.finding: Methods of the systematic part: searches from 1980 to August 2014 following PRISMA; inclusion of adult population samples, IHD by ICD codes, case-control or cohort designs, a drinking group under 30 g/day defined by the presence or absence of episodic heavy drinking, and a comparison with lifetime abstainers; English, German or Spanish only; search and data abstraction by the first author, with eligibility of full texts agreed by both authors; primary authors not contacted.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (Methods); Methods › Searches; Methods › Meta-analysis › Inclusion and exclusion criteria; Methods › Meta-analysis › Data abstraction

key_findings.finding: Seven studies met the criteria. Against lifetime abstainers, IHD incidence (mortality and morbidity combined) was lower in drinkers averaging under 30 g/day without heavy drinking occasions, RR 0.64 (95% CI 0.53 to 0.71), and not different in drinkers with the same average intake and heavy drinking occasions, 1.12 (0.91 to 1.37).
key_findings.locator: Abstract (Results); Results and discussion › Meta-analysis on drinking pattern among moderate alcohol drinkers, 1st paragraph; Figure 2 (legend)
key_findings.note: The interval 0.53 to 0.71 is not symmetric around 0.64 on the log scale (see reporting issues). Figure 2 and the forest plots in the supplement were not read for values.

key_findings.finding: Heterogeneity was low (I² 10% without and 0% with heavy drinking occasions); Egger's test P = 0.35 and 0.58; no single study had a large influence; all seven studies adjusted for age and smoking, five for education or other socio-economic indicators, four each for body mass index and marital status.
key_findings.locator: Results and discussion › Meta-analysis on drinking pattern among moderate alcohol drinkers, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The relative risk between the two drinking groups (with against without heavy drinking occasions) was 1.75 (1.36 to 2.25), higher than the 1.45 of the authors' 2010 meta-analysis; the authors read this as the impact of episodic heavy drinking being greatest at low average intake.
key_findings.locator: Results and discussion › Meta-analysis on drinking pattern among moderate alcohol drinkers, 2nd paragraph; Results and discussion › Drinking pattern, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: 1.75 equals 1.12 divided by 0.64 (editors' arithmetic); how its interval was computed is not described.

key_findings.finding: From the authors' 2011 meta-analysis of 54 studies, as reported here: former drinkers had higher IHD mortality than lifetime abstainers, women 1.54 (1.17 to 2.03) and men 1.25 (1.15 to 1.36); the definition of lifetime abstention did not change this.
key_findings.locator: Results and discussion › Lifetime abstainers and former drinkers, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Second-hand from the authors' own earlier meta-analysis (ref. 33).

key_findings.finding: From the authors' 2014 Open Heart meta-analysis, as reported here: men drinking 60 g/day or more had IHD mortality similar to lifetime abstainers (1.00, 0.74 to 1.36) and IHD incidence 1.04 (0.83 to 1.31). Against current non-drinkers, Ronksley et al. (2011) had reported 0.76 (0.52 to 1.09) for IHD incidence and 0.75 (0.63 to 0.89) for IHD mortality above 60 g/day, which the authors attribute to the choice of reference group.
key_findings.locator: Results and discussion › Average alcohol consumption, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
key_findings.note: Second-hand (refs 18 and 39). The Ronksley incidence estimate cited is itself not significant.

key_findings.finding: From the authors' 2014 meta-analysis of people treated for alcohol use disorder, as reported here: IHD mortality against the general population, men 1.62 (1.34 to 1.95), women 2.09 (1.28 to 3.41); the abstract summarizes this as a 1.5- to 2-fold risk.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (Results); Results and discussion › Average alcohol consumption, 4th paragraph
key_findings.note: The comparator is the general population, not lifetime abstainers.

key_findings.finding: The narrative summarizes the authors' 2012 meta-analysis as clearly showing a beneficial association against lifetime abstainers when all studies were included, with all pooled IHD estimates significant at one to two drinks a day (point estimates 0.69 to 0.81), and with women showing slightly stronger associations and an earlier upturn than men.
key_findings.locator: Results and discussion › Average alcohol consumption, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: These figures match Table 4 (all studies) of the 2012 paper; its fully stratified Table 2, with non-significant estimates for men's mortality at about 1 and 2 drinks, is not mentioned (card sc_roerecke_2012).

key_findings.finding: Russian studies, taking low-level drinkers rather than lifetime abstainers as the reference, report substantially raised IHD risk in heavy drinkers; the authors' speculative re-scaling, assuming the Russian reference group (about 4.6 g/day) has the risk of low-level drinkers elsewhere (0.81), gives 1.58 (1.48 to 1.69), and assuming benefit in 25% of the population gives 1.36 (1.13 to 1.64) for men treated for alcohol use disorder.
key_findings.locator: Results and discussion › Average alcohol consumption, 5th and 6th paragraphs; Figure 1 (legend)
key_findings.note: Labelled by the authors as speculation; the method is not described.

key_findings.finding: On confounding, the narrative states that adding confounders changed pooled estimates little (citing Ronksley et al. and a pooled analysis of eight cohorts), that an inverse or J-shaped relation was seen in never or non-smokers in all but one population study, that evidence in smokers is mixed, and that evidence by physical activity and body mass index is sparse.
key_findings.locator: Results and discussion › Confounding from other risk factors for ischemic heart disease, 1st paragraph; › Smoking, 2nd paragraph; › Other confounding factors, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Experimental evidence: no long-term randomized studies of alcohol and IHD exist; short-term studies show dose-dependent effects on surrogate markers (higher HDL cholesterol, less platelet activation, lower fibrinogen, anti-inflammatory effects), with HDL also raised by regular heavy drinking and highest in people with alcohol use disorder. The Mendelian randomization study of Holmes et al. (2014), using the ADH1B variant rs1229984, concluded there was no protective effect; the authors argue it is hard to compare with the epidemiology because the variant was also linked to less binge drinking.
key_findings.locator: Results and discussion › Experimental evidence, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The conclusions state that using current abstainers as the reference leads to systematic bias, that against lifetime abstainers the relation follows a J-curve that turns detrimental at lower intakes in women, that episodic and chronic heavy drinking negate any beneficial association, that the relationship fulfils all of Hill's criteria, that uptake of drinking should not be considered for preventing IHD, and that for public policy no amount of drinking is safe.
key_findings.note: The authors' conclusions, appraised in the interpretation gap.

reporting_issues.issue: The pooled estimate for drinkers without heavy drinking occasions, 0.64 (0.53 to 0.71), given identically in the abstract and the results, is not symmetric on the log scale: the geometric midpoint of the interval is 0.61, and a lower limit of 0.53 would imply an upper limit of about 0.77 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract (Results); Results and discussion › Meta-analysis on drinking pattern among moderate alcohol drinkers, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The point estimate or one of the limits is probably misprinted; Figure 2 (image) and the supplement could not be checked. Claims should quote the figures as printed and note the inconsistency.

reporting_issues.issue: How the ratio of 1.75 (1.36 to 2.25) between the two drinking groups was obtained is not described; it equals the ratio of the two pooled estimates, which share lifetime-abstainer reference groups within studies.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results and discussion › Meta-analysis on drinking pattern among moderate alcohol drinkers, 2nd paragraph; Methods › Meta-analysis › Statistical analysis
reporting_issues.consequence: The interval of the ratio cannot be checked and may not allow for the correlation between the two estimates.

reporting_issues.issue: Essential details of the systematic part are only in Additional file 1: the databases searched, the search strings, the definition of a heavy drinking occasion, the identities, designs, settings and sizes of the seven studies, and their forest plots; the Methods also omit the year of the search end date (August 2014 is given only in the abstract).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Searches; Results and discussion › Meta-analysis on drinking pattern among moderate alcohol drinkers, 1st paragraph; Additional file 1 (description)
reporting_issues.consequence: The pooled estimates cannot be appraised from the article; the exposure (what counted as heavy drinking occasions) cannot be stated in a claim without the supplement.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract's Methods describe comparisons against lifetime abstainers, and its Results give a 1.5- to 2-fold IHD risk in people with alcohol use disorder; the text's figures (men 1.62, women 2.09) are against the general population.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract (Methods, Results); Results and discussion › Average alcohol consumption, 4th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: A claim based on the abstract would misstate the comparator of the alcohol-use-disorder estimates.

reporting_issues.issue: The narrative says a beneficial association among chronic heavy drinkers appears only with current abstainers as the reference and gives Ronksley et al.'s estimates as the example, but one of the two, 0.76 (0.52 to 1.09) for IHD incidence, is not significant.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results and discussion › Average alcohol consumption, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Only the mortality estimate (0.75, 0.63 to 0.89) illustrates the point.

reporting_issues.issue: Reference list errors: ref. 33 (the authors' former-drinker meta-analysis, source of the 1.54 and 1.25) is printed as American Journal of Epidemiology 2011, volume 73, while the same article is cited with volume 173 in the authors' 2012 review; ref. 36 is dated 2012 although its DOI carries a 1998 identifier.
reporting_issues.consequence: Bibliographic only; no effect on the numbers.
